name: zlib-ng
workload: General deflate/inflate throughput plus CRC32-B and Adler32 checksum computation on x86-64, using SIMD (SSE2/SSE4.1/PCLMULQDQ/AVX2/AVX512) and ARMv8 PMULL+EOR3 code paths as a drop-in zlib replacement
claimed_speedup: "Major speed improvements, x86-64 can be about 4x faster than stock zlib for example."
tradeoffs: Drop-in ABI-compatible replacement for zlib; installing system-wide risks breaking other software if misconfigured. CRC32/Adler32 SIMD paths require runtime CPU feature detection.
caveats: The "4x" figure is a first-party README claim with no stated CPU model, compiler, or flags, and covers overall zlib throughput (compression+decompression+checksums), not an isolated CRC32-only number.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "zlib-ng" (surfaced while chasing the CRC32 shootout thread)

name: stb_zip (CRC32 routine)
workload: CRC32 checksum of a 1GB in-memory buffer
claimed_speedup: CRC32 of 1GB data: 0.2 sec (stb_zip) vs 1.1 sec (miniz 3.0) = 5.5x
tradeoffs: Header-only single-file C library; only supports store/deflate ZIP entries, not a general-purpose zlib replacement.
caveats: First-party single-table README benchmark; miniz is a widely-used lightweight zlib-compatible library but is not the canonical zlib CRC32 baseline itself, and compiler/flags are unstated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "crc32 zlib"

name: komrad36/CRC ("Golden" hardware-accelerated CRC32)
baseline: CRC32 (naive/tabular byte-at-a-time implementation, of the kind used by zlib and most CRC32 libraries)
workload: CRC32 checksum of an in-memory buffer of random data on x86, comparing 13 progressively optimized implementations from bitwise through 16-byte tabular to a 3-way-parallel PCLMULQDQ-folding "Golden" hardware-accelerated version
claimed_speedup: Golden (hardware-accelerated, 3-way parallel PCLMULQDQ folding): ~62 bits/cycle vs 16-byte tabular baseline ~8 bits/cycle (~7.75x), and >150x vs the naive bitwise implementation
tradeoffs: Hardware-accelerated "Golden" path requires SSE4.2 (crc32 instruction) plus PCLMULQDQ; earlier tabular options in the same repo are the portable fallback for non-x86/embedded targets.
caveats: README is a first-party educational derivation with a self-reported bits-per-cycle table; no specific CPU model or compiler/flags are given, so numbers are illustrative rather than reproducible as stated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "crc32 fast" -> "Fastest CRC32 for x86"

name: Faster CRC32 on Apple M1 (dougallj, PMULL multi-chain)
workload: CRC32 checksum throughput on Apple M1, using PMULL polynomial-multiply with independent latency chains (NEON/ARM64), building on Intel's 2009 PCLMULQDQ folding technique
claimed_speedup: ~70GB/s (up to ~75GB/s with adjusted fusion pairs) vs zlib's ~30GB/s on the same M1 (~2.3x); hardware CRC32X instruction alone tops out at ~25.6GB/s theoretical
stars_or_usage: 343 HN points; follow-on state-of-the-art (corsix/fast-crc32, already catalogued) is a direct descendant of this work
tradeoffs: ARM64/NEON-specific technique (PMULL + fusion pairs tuned to Apple's execution ports); not portable to x86 as written.
caveats: Distributed only as a GitHub gist with an "AS IS" disclaimer, no formal OSI license, and no compiler/flags stated; author's own first-party blog post rather than an independent benchmark.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "crc32 fast" -> "Faster CRC32 on the Apple M1"

name: fast-base64 (mitschabaude)
baseline: the fastest existing JS base64 implementation (unnamed; also compared against native atob()/btoa())
workload: Converting between base64 strings and Uint8Array of 100kB to 100MB, in-browser and in Node/Deno, hand-written WASM with SIMD
claimed_speedup: "~20x faster than the fastest JS implementation on the first 100kB of input", "~2-3x faster than the fastest JS on the first 100MB"
tradeoffs: Async API for the fastest (SIMD Wasm) variant; smaller/sync variants trade 2-100x speed for size or synchronicity. Threaded variants were found to be no faster except for >1MB payloads in pure JS.
caveats: "the fastest JS implementation" is not a specific named library, so the baseline is fuzzy; not usable directly from C++ (JS/Wasm only), included per the any-language allowance.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "SIMD base64"

name: klauspost/crc32 (AVX512 IEEE CRC32)
workload: IEEE CRC32 checksum of 512B-32kB buffers at various memory alignments, drop-in replacement for Go's hash/crc32 package using AVX512 above a 1KB input-size threshold
claimed_speedup: 2.09x-2.35x faster at 1kB-32kB sizes, e.g. 45.6-48.6 GB/s (new, AVX512) vs 19.9-21.9 GB/s (old); negligible change at 512B where AVX512 is not yet enabled
tradeoffs: Go-only (not usable from C++ directly); AVX512 path only activates above 1KB inputs, so small-message workloads see no speedup and may pay ramp-up cost.
caveats: CPU model is stated but compiler version/flags are only implied (Go 1.24); benchmark table is the project's own README, not an independently run suite.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "crc32 fast" -> "CRC32 hash with x64 optimizations"

name: hx (binary-to-hex-simd, NEON table lookup)
workload: Converting 12 MiB of binary data to ASCII hexadecimal, comparing byte-by-byte, portable_simd, and hand-written NEON table-lookup (neon_tbl) implementations
claimed_speedup: neon_tbl: 6.24 GiB/s vs byte_by_byte: 0.79 GiB/s (~7.9x); best run measured 6.53 GiB/s
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook (author notes it was not a quiet machine, on battery power)
tradeoffs: ARM64/NEON-specific hand-written assembly; a learning/hobby project rather than a hardened library, no fallback dispatch story for other ISAs shown in README.
caveats: Author explicitly says the benchmark environment was noisy ("take these results with a grain of salt"); baseline is an internal naive implementation in the same repo, not a separate named hex library.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "hex simd"

name: turbobase64 (Cython/Python bindings for Turbo-Base64)
workload: Python-level base64 encode/decode of byte strings, dispatching at runtime to scalar/SSSE3/AVX/AVX2/AVX512-VBMI C kernels
claimed_speedup: "20-30x faster than the standard library"; "Benchmarks faster than any other C base64 library" (per project's own benchmark.py chart)
tradeoffs: Adds a Python/Cython layer over the underlying C SIMD kernels; the "faster than any other C library" claim is only presented as a chart image, not tabulated numbers, in the README.
caveats: The underlying SIMD codec is powturbo/Turbo-Base64, which is already catalogued (excluded per KNOWN_LIST); this entry's distinct contribution is the separate Python/Cython binding repo and its own comparative benchmark, not new SIMD code. No CPU/compiler stated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "fastest base64 library"
